title: Impact Calculus
subtitle: Argument Foundations · Mission 07
tagline: Both teams say bad things will happen. The judge picks {{amber:one}}. Learn the {{amber:P-T-M}} weighers that tell the judge whose impact matters more.

slides.headline: ⚖️ WHOSE IMPACT WINS?
body: Two teams. Both say scary things will happen if the other one wins.
Team A: *{{cyan:"The economy will lose 100 jobs."}}* 💼
Team B: *{{amber:"A million people will die."}}* 💀
Which one is worse? **Obvious**, right? That choice you just made in your head — that's {{amber:impact calculus}}. ⚖️
But real rounds are trickier. Sometimes both impacts sound huge. If you don't tell the judge {{amber:which one wins}}, the judge has to guess. And guessing is bad for you.

items.label: Define {{amber:impact calculus}} and why every rebuttal needs it
Master the three weighers: {{amber:Probability · Timeframe · Magnitude}}
Build a real impact calc line the judge can flow

slides.definition: {{amber:Impact calculus}} (or *impact calc*) is comparing {{cyan:your}} impact to {{amber:the other team's}} impact — and telling the judge {{amber:which one matters more}}. It's how you win a round when both sides sound scary. ⚖️
slides.plainWords: You don't just say your impact is bad. You say *why yours is worse than theirs*. The judge is keeping score — help them.
slides.analogy: Imagine two kids fighting over the last cookie, both yelling *"I'm hungrier!"* The parent has no idea who to give it to. But if one kid says *"I haven't eaten all day and she just had lunch,"* — now the parent has a reason to pick. Impact calc = giving the judge a {{amber:reason to pick you}}. 🍪

slides.headline: P-T-M: THE THREE WEIGHERS
slides.intro: There are three ways to prove your impact is worse than theirs. You don't have to win all three — {{amber:winning one clearly}} is usually enough. Every rebuttal should end with at least one.

cards.name: P — PROBABILITY
cards.description: How {{amber:likely}} is your impact to actually happen? A 100% sure thing beats a wild guess every time.

example.label: Think of it like
example.text: Rain vs. a meteor hitting a baseball game. The meteor's worse — but rain is {{amber:way more likely}}. Rain wins on Probability.

cards.name: T — TIMEFRAME
cards.description: How {{amber:soon}} does your impact hit? A bad thing next week beats a bad thing in 50 years.

example.label: Think of it like
example.text: A bad grade on tomorrow's test vs. a bad grade in a college class ten years from now. Tomorrow's grade wins on {{amber:Timeframe}} — it hits {{amber:now}}.

cards.name: M — MAGNITUDE
cards.description: How {{amber:big}} is your impact? How many people? How badly hurt? Millions beats dozens. Death beats inconvenience.

example.label: Think of it like
example.text: One kid missing recess vs. the {{amber:whole school}} missing recess. Same problem — but the whole school is a way bigger deal. Magnitude wins.

slides.headline: ⚡ HOW TO SAY IT IN A ROUND
slides.intro: Knowing P-T-M isn't enough. You have to {{amber:say it out loud}} so the judge writes it down. Every rebuttal should have a line like this. Here's the shape.

rows.name: 1️⃣ Name the weigher
rows.description: Start by telling the judge {{amber:which weigher}} you're using. Don't make them guess. Say the word.

rows.name: 2️⃣ Compare the two impacts
rows.description: Now put {{cyan:your}} impact next to {{amber:their}} impact — directly. Numbers help. Timeframes help. Sources help.

counter.label: Sounds like
counter.text: *"...our card is peer-reviewed, and their impact is a prediction with no evidence."*

rows.name: 3️⃣ Tell the judge how to vote
rows.description: End with the {{amber:ballot instruction}}. The judge needs to hear the words *"vote AFF"* or *"vote NEG"* connected to your impact calc.

counter.label: Sounds like
counter.text: *"Because our impact is more likely, you vote AFF."* 🗳️

rows.name: ⭐ Pro move: stack the weighers
rows.description: One weigher wins the argument. {{amber:Two or three}} weighers wins the round. If you can hit Probability *and* Timeframe *and* Magnitude, the judge has nowhere to go.

counter.label: Sounds like
counter.text: *"Our impact is more likely (P), it happens sooner (T), and it kills more people (M). Every weigher goes AFF."*

prompt.label: WEIGHER MATCH
prompt.scenario: Three quick scenarios. Match each one to the weigher it's using.
prompt.question: Drag each scenario on the left to the right {{amber:weigher}} on the right.

items.text: *"Our impact happens next year. Theirs takes 50 years to hit."*
*"Our card is from a peer-reviewed study. Theirs is a guess from a blog."*
*"Our impact hurts 68,000 people a year. Theirs hurts a few dozen."*

correct.title: ✓ WEIGHERS LOCKED IN
body: Clean match. When someone talks about *when* → {{cyan:Timeframe}}. When they talk about *how sure* → {{amber:Probability}}. When they talk about *how many / how bad* → {{amber:Magnitude}}. Every impact calc line uses at least one of these three. ⚖️
correct.followup: **Pro move:** In a real rebuttal, name the weigher {{amber:out loud}} — *"we outweigh on Probability"* — before you compare. The judge is writing down keywords, and *Probability / Timeframe / Magnitude* are the ones they're listening for.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ WEIGHERS CROSSED
body: Quick test: is the sentence about {{cyan:when}} it happens → **Timeframe**. About {{amber:how sure}} it is → **Probability**. About {{amber:how big / how many}} → **Magnitude**. Read each scenario and ask which question it's answering.

prompt.label: THE METEOR TEST
prompt.scenario:
It's the middle of a baseball game. Two things could ruin it:

☔ Some **rain** (annoying, but the game gets rescheduled)
☄️ A **meteor** hitting the field (devastating — but astronomically unlikely)
prompt.question: If you were the *rain* team, which weigher would you use to win against the meteor team?

options.text: Magnitude — rain affects more people than a meteor
Probability — rain is way more likely to actually happen
Timeframe — rain and meteors both happen instantly
None — the meteor team wins automatically because it's worse

correct.title: ✓ CLEAN HIT
body: Exactly. A meteor would be devastating — but it's basically {{amber:never going to happen}}. Rain is a near-certainty. When one impact is {{amber:way more likely}} than the other, you win on {{amber:Probability}}. 🎯
correct.followup: **Big lesson:** A {{amber:huge scary impact}} with almost no chance of happening loses to a {{cyan:smaller impact that will definitely happen}}. This is how Neg teams beat sci-fi Aff impacts every day.

a.title: ✕ WRONG WEIGHER
body: A meteor would hurt more people than rain — so you'd {{amber:lose}} on Magnitude, not win. The whole point is that rain wins because it's {{amber:more likely}}, not because it's bigger.

c.title: ✕ NOT ABOUT TIMING
body: Timeframe is about {{cyan:how soon}} an impact hits, not how fast the event is. Both rain and meteors hit the same day — Timeframe doesn't help either side. The difference is {{amber:Probability}}.

d.title: ✕ THAT'S NOT HOW IT WORKS
body: "It's worse" isn't automatic — it's only Magnitude. And Magnitude can lose to {{amber:Probability}}. If the meteor is 1-in-a-billion, rain wins the round.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan:B — Probability}}. Rain is nearly certain; a meteor is nearly impossible. When your impact is {{amber:way more likely}}, that's the weigher you use.

prompt.label: IMPACT CALC TRIAGE
prompt.scenario: You're prepping your rebuttal. Six impact calc lines are on your notes — but they're jumbled. Sort each one into the weigher it's using: {{amber:PROBABILITY}}, {{cyan:TIMEFRAME}}, or {{amber:MAGNITUDE}}.
prompt.question: Drop each line into the right bin.

cards.text: *"Theirs takes 20 years to materialize. Ours starts on day one."*
*"Our evidence is peer-reviewed; theirs is speculation."*
*"Their impact requires five things to go wrong in a row. Ours only needs one."*
*"The plan takes effect immediately after passage."*

correct.title: ✓ SORTED CLEAN
body: That's the triage a good rebuttalist does before every speech. {{amber:Probability}} lines talk about *evidence quality* or *chain of events*. {{cyan:Timeframe}} lines talk about *when*. {{amber:Magnitude}} lines talk about *how many / how bad*.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** Before your rebuttal, group your best impact calc lines by weigher. Then run through P → T → M in order. If you've got a line in every bin, {{amber:you've got a knockout rebuttal}}.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ RE-TRIAGE
body: Litmus test for each card: does it talk about {{amber:how sure}} something is (evidence, chain of causes) → **Probability**. About {{cyan:when}} → **Timeframe**. About {{amber:how big or how many}} → **Magnitude**.

prompt.label: BUILD THE IMPACT CALC
prompt.scenario:
You're the AFF. Your impact: {{cyan:*68,000 people die every year from lack of health insurance.*}} Their impact: {{amber:*a recession might happen in 20 years if the plan passes.*}}

Build your impact calc line by filling in the three weighers.
prompt.question: Drop the right word into each blank.

slides.template:
Our impact outweighs on {{1}} — 68,000 deaths a year is huge.

We also outweigh on {{2}} — our impact happens NOW, theirs takes 20 years.

And we outweigh on {{3}} — deaths from lack of insurance are documented; their recession is speculation.

Vote AFF.

blanks.hint: Documented vs. speculation — that's about {{amber:how likely}}.

correct.title: ✓ FULL-STACK IMPACT CALC
body: That's a knockout rebuttal. You just hit {{amber:all three weighers}} in a row and told the judge exactly how to vote. Magnitude (huge number), Timeframe (now vs. later), Probability (documented vs. guess) — every weigher goes AFF. ⚖️
correct.followup: **Pro tip:** You don't always get all three. But when you do — {{amber:say all three out loud}}. Each weigher is a separate reason for the judge to vote your way. Stack them.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ REBUILD
body: Three checkpoints: {{amber:how many}} = **Magnitude**. {{cyan:when}} = **Timeframe**. {{amber:how likely}} = **Probability**. Re-read each sentence and ask which question it's answering.

prompt.label: BIG IDEA CHECK
prompt.question: 🎯 Why can't you just skip impact calculus and let the judge decide whose impact is worse?

options.text: If you don't compare, the judge has to guess — and guesses go against you
Judges aren't allowed to compare impacts on their own
The bigger impact automatically wins without you saying anything
Impact calc is optional — most rounds don't need it

correct.title: ✓ THAT'S THE WHOLE POINT
body: Exactly. Judges are trained to only decide based on what teams {{amber:actually say}}. If you don't do impact calc, the judge is forced to pick between two scary impacts with no framework — and that guess {{amber:almost always goes to the other team}}. ⚖️
correct.followup: **Pro tip:** This is why every rebuttal should end with impact calc. It's not a bonus — it's the {{amber:closing argument}} of your speech. No impact calc = no clean way for the judge to vote for you.

b.title: ✕ JUDGES CAN COMPARE
body: Judges *can* compare impacts on their own — that's the problem. If you don't guide them, they'll compare {{amber:however they feel like}}, which is usually not in your favor.

c.title: ✕ NOT AUTOMATIC
body: "Bigger" only counts if you {{amber:say it out loud}} and prove it. A huge impact with no calc loses to a smaller impact with strong calc. Every time.

d.title: ✕ NOT OPTIONAL
body: Impact calc isn't optional at the varsity level and isn't optional at the novice level either. Every {{amber:rebuttal}} — 1AR, 2NR, 2AR — should end with it.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan:A}}. Without impact calc, the judge has to guess — and their guess almost never picks the team that stayed silent.

slides.headline: IMPACT CALC LOCKED IN ⚖️
slides.subtext: You've got the three weighers: {{amber:Probability}} (how likely?), {{cyan:Timeframe}} (how soon?), {{amber:Magnitude}} (how big?). Win one clearly and you win the argument. Win all three and you win the round. Every rebuttal ends with impact calc now — no exceptions.
